The museum opened on a Tuesday because nobody could agree on a suitable date, and Tuesday was already happening.

It occupied the ground floor of a former furniture shop between a pharmacy and a place that repaired phones. Above the entrance, someone had painted THE MUSEUM OF UNFINISHED THINGS. The last letter remained an outline. People assumed this was intentional. The painter, who had gone to buy a sandwich and never returned, was pleased to hear it.

At first, the collection was small.

There was a sweater with one sleeve, donated by a woman who said she had stopped loving the intended recipient somewhere around the elbow. There was a notebook containing the first sentences of forty-three novels. There was a wooden boat without a mast, a crossword abandoned in 1987, and an envelope addressed in careful handwriting but never stamped.

The envelope attracted the most attention. Visitors leaned toward it as though paper could whisper.

“Can we read the letter?” they asked.

“There is no letter,” said Mara, the museum’s only employee.

This disappointed people more than she expected. They wanted a confession interrupted by fear, an apology arriving too late. The idea that someone had addressed an envelope before knowing what to say seemed to them like poor planning rather than heartbreak.

Mara understood both interpretations.

She had taken the job after leaving architecture school with one semester remaining. When asked why she had left, she gave different answers depending on how long the questioner appeared willing to listen. Money was the shortest answer. Exhaustion was longer. The longest involved a hospital corridor, her father’s slippers, and a building she had designed on paper in which every room received the morning sun.

None of these answers was false.

Every morning, she unlocked the museum at ten, switched on the lights, and checked the donation box. Most offerings were ordinary: embroidery, half-carved spoons, diaries that ended in February. Some were difficult to classify. One man brought a jar of sourdough starter and insisted it was a future loaf. A child submitted a stone she had intended to throw into the sea.

“Why didn’t you?” Mara asked.

“I decided to keep it.”

“Then perhaps you finished deciding.”

The child considered this, took back the stone, and left looking satisfied.

By November, the museum had become unexpectedly popular. A newspaper called it “a tender indictment of productivity.” A business magazine called it “a bold new cultural concept.” Someone offered to sponsor a room devoted to abandoned fitness goals.

Mara declined the sponsorship. She was not certain why, except that the proposed room came with mirrors.

The visitors behaved differently from visitors in other museums. They rarely asked what anything was worth. Instead, they stood before a half-finished quilt and described their aunt, or pointed at an unassembled radio and went quiet. They recognized things.

One afternoon, an elderly man arrived carrying a door.

It was an interior door, painted green, with a brass handle and three pencil marks near the frame. He maneuvered it through the entrance without asking for help, then stood beside it, breathing hard.

“I can’t accept building materials,” Mara said.

“It isn’t building materials.”

He touched the pencil marks.

“My wife measured our daughter here. We were going to keep doing it.”

Mara waited.

“She grew up,” he said. “Nothing tragic. We moved. Then we moved again. I kept bringing the door.”

“What’s unfinished?”

He looked irritated, then embarrassed.

“I suppose I thought there would be more marks.”

They found a place for it near the window.

That evening, Mara stayed after closing. Outside, the pharmacy sign flickered. Rain gathered along the bottom of the glass.

She walked through the collection without her clipboard.

Certain objects had begun to trouble her. Not because they were sad, but because the museum gave them a permanence their owners had never intended. A failed attempt became an exhibit. A hesitation acquired a label. People who might someday finish their sweaters now visited them on weekends.

The next morning, she placed a small table beside the entrance. On it were scissors, glue, pencils, a sewing kit, and a sign:

YOU MAY ASK FOR YOUR THING BACK.

The board of trustees objected. There were only three trustees, and one had joined because he misunderstood the word “board,” but their objections were serious. Museums preserved things. Museums did not encourage collections to wander away.

Mara suggested they try it for a month.

The woman reclaimed her sweater, unraveled the sleeve, and made a hat for herself. The novelist took his notebook home, then returned it two weeks later with one additional sentence. The man with the door visited twice, ran his thumb over the brass handle, and left it where it was.

Other visitors brought tools but no donations. A retired electrician repaired the lighting above the exhibits. The missing painter returned and filled in the final letter.

In December, Mara retrieved her architectural drawings from a cupboard. She spread them across the museum floor after closing and examined the impossible windows, the generous staircases, the rooms washed clean with sunlight.

She did not enroll again that night. She did not suddenly understand her life. She found an error in the placement of a wall, sharpened a pencil, and corrected it.

Then she measured the museum.

The entrance was awkward for wheelchairs. The reading corner needed better light. There was space behind the office for a small workshop, if the shelves could be moved.

When she finally stood up, her knees hurt. She stacked the drawings on her desk rather than returning them to the cupboard.

Outside, the phone repair shop was closing. Its owner struggled with his shutter, and Mara crossed the pavement to help. Together they pulled until it caught.

“Finished?” he asked.

“For tonight,” she said.

He nodded, accepting the distinction, and they went their separate ways.
